analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and extends payroll taxes to all earnings, including above the current cap.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without action in the House Ways and Means Committee since its referral in May 2025, with no cosponsors and no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill increases Social Security benefits for people who earned low wages over a lifetime, for beneficiaries who have collected benefits for many years, and for children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers who are full-time college students up to age 26. To pay for it, the bill gradually applies Social Security payroll taxes to all earnings by 2035, removing the cap that currently exempts wages above $176,100, and raises the payroll tax rate slightly from 6.2% to 6.5% for both workers and employers. It also makes sure the benefit increases don't count as income against people receiving other government aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners, who would get a guaranteed minimum benefit tied to the poverty line based on years worked, including years spent caring for young children; people who have received Social Security for 16 or more years, who would get a growing boost up to 5% of their benefit; and students up to age 26 whose parent is retired, disabled, or deceased, who would keep receiving benefits while in college full time.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a special minimum benefit so workers with 30 or more years in the workforce (counting up to five years of child care) are guaranteed at least 100% of the poverty guideline in benefits, phased in from 36.7% at 11 years of work.
Adds a new benefit increase for anyone who has been eligible for Social Security for 16 years or more, rising from 20% to a full 5% of the benefit amount at 20 years or longer.
Extends child's benefits through age 26 for full-time post-secondary students, up from the current cutoff around age 19 for high school students.

Ensures the benefit increases are not counted as income or resources when determining eligibility for other federal, state, or locally funded assistance programs, so higher Social Security checks do not cost someone their food or housing assistance.

Phases out the taxable maximum so payroll taxes apply to all earnings by 2035, and revises the benefit formula to credit some of those higher earnings, which improves Social Security's long-term finances.

analysis.who_pays: High-income workers and their employers. Wages above the taxable maximum would be progressively brought into the payroll tax base over ten years, and every worker and employer would see the tax rate rise in small steps from 6.2% to 6.5% (12.5% to 13.0% for the self-employed) by 2031.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the payroll tax rate on all workers and employers, from 6.2% to 6.5% over six years, which modestly reduces take-home pay for every wage earner, not just high earners.

Applying payroll taxes to earnings above the cap while crediting only a small additional benefit rate (3% on earnings above the base) weakens the traditional one-to-one link between what high earners pay in and what they get out, which critics of such proposals describe as moving Social Security away from an earned-benefit model toward a redistributive one.
The full removal of the taxable maximum by 2035, with only a partial benefit credit above it, means the highest earners would face the largest new tax burden in the program's structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers targeted help to the poorest beneficiaries and improves the program's finances by asking more from those with the highest earnings, but it does so by raising a payroll tax that falls on every worker and employer in small increments. The main cost is concentrated on high earners; the broad tax increase is modest but real. For an honest supporter, the tradeoff is a small across-the-board pay cut for all workers in exchange for a stronger benefit floor and better solvency.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in May 2025 and has seen no further action, hearing, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
As of the latest action record, the committee has not held a markup or scheduled the bill for a floor vote, and no vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, no one has gained or lost anything yet. High earners keep the current tax cap in place, and low-income beneficiaries get none of the proposed increases.

for.name: Rep. Gwen Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Enhancement and Protection Act of 2025 on May 20, 2025.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on May 20, 2025 — no markup, hearing, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote has occurred, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: High-income earners (wages above the taxable maximum)
industries.note: Wages above $176,100 would be brought into the Social Security tax base over ten years, reaching all earnings by 2035. This group's interest in keeping the cap runs directly against the bill's funding for benefit increases for low and long-term beneficiaries.
The employer share of the payroll tax rises in small steps from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2031, a modest labor cost increase, and employers of high earners face taxes on previously exempt wages.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action eight months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance on its own. It could in principle be folded into a broader Social Security or budget package, but standalone bills introduced by a single member rarely get a markup or floor vote.
